title: Just a Little Longer
excerpt: Few lives fall apart in a day. Proverbs on the slow drift of just a little longer, and the rest that Jesus gives.

blocks.text: Think of the thing that has been sitting on your list the longest.

Maybe it's a phone call you keep meaning to make. A conversation you know you need to have. A project you've been "about to start" since spring. An apology. A budget. A doctor's appointment. A decision. It's not that you've decided against it. You haven't. You just haven't done it *yet*, and today doesn't feel quite right, so you'll get to it tomorrow. Or next week. After things calm down.

Nobody wakes up and decides to let their life quietly fall apart. But one of the oldest observations in Proverbs is that this is exactly how it happens, not through a dramatic decision, but through a long series of "just a little longer."
The Field Along the Road
The writer of Proverbs tells a short story about a walk he took one day.

"I went past the field of a sluggard, past the vineyard of someone who has no sense; thorns had come up everywhere, the ground was covered with weeds, and the stone wall was in ruins" (Proverbs 24:30–31).

It's a simple picture. There was a field that used to be worth something. Someone had planted it, built a wall around it, and put real effort into it once. And now it's overgrown. The wall has collapsed. The weeds have taken over.

What I love is the next line: "I applied my heart to what I observed and learned a lesson from what I saw" (24:32). He doesn't just walk past and shake his head. He stops, and he asks how a field gets like this.
And his answer is almost anticlimactic:

verses: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest — and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man.

blocks.text: That's it. No catastrophe. No single day when everything fell apart. Just *a little* sleep, *a little* slumber, *a little* folding of the hands. Each one tiny. Each one reasonable. Each one easy to justify. And then, one day, the thief shows up, and the field is gone.
The writer liked this line so much that he used it twice. It appears almost word for word back in chapter 6, as part of a famous rebuke.
Learning from an Ant
"Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise!" (6:6).

It's a funny image, being sent to school by an insect. But the lesson is sharp. "It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest" (6:7–8).

The ant has no boss standing over her. No deadline, no notification, no one to be accountable to. And she still does the work, because she understands something we often forget: the season for preparing is not the season when you need what you prepared. The ant gathers in summer because winter is coming. Procrastination's whole trick is convincing you that there's plenty of summer left.

Then Proverbs asks a pair of questions that feel uncomfortably personal: "How long will you lie there? When will you get up from your sleep?" (6:9). It's not a harsh question, really. It's the kind of question you'd want a good friend to ask.
Why We Really Drift
Here's where I want to be careful, because it's easy to read passages like this and walk away feeling like you've been called lazy. And that's not quite the whole picture.

A lot of procrastination isn't laziness at all. It's fear. Fear that we'll do it badly. Fear of the conversation. Fear that we'll try and fail, which feels worse than never trying. Sometimes it's simply overwhelm, a task so big we don't know where to begin. Proverbs doesn't ignore this. Elsewhere it describes a man who won't leave the house because "there's a lion in the road!" (26:13). The excuse sounds reasonable. The lion may not even be real. But the effect is the same: a life that never leaves the doorway.

It's also worth saying that Proverbs isn't against rest. Scripture is full of Sabbath, of Jesus withdrawing to quiet places, of sleep as a gift from God. The difference is in what the rest is *for.* Rest that refuels you is a gift. "Just a little longer" that you use to avoid something you know you need to face is something else. You usually know which one you're doing.

And notice the real danger the passage describes. It isn't that you'll miss a deadline. It's that scarcity will come "like a thief." You won't see it coming. You won't hear it break in. You'll just look up one day and find something was taken that you never noticed leaving.
Small Starts, Not Giant Leaps

If you're sitting with something you've been avoiding, Proverbs' solution isn't a dramatic overhaul. It's the same size as the problem. The slow drift happened one small delay at a time, and it turns around one small start at a time.

You don't have to fix the whole field today. You just have to pull one weed. Send the one email. Make the one call. Open the document and write one bad paragraph. The ant doesn't build the whole colony in an afternoon. She carries one crumb, and then another. Momentum is built from beginnings, not finishes.

And be gentle with yourself about it. The goal isn't to shame yourself into action. Shame is a terrible motivator and usually just feeds the avoidance. The goal is to take one step, and let the step make the next one a little easier.
The Delay That Matters Most
But there's one kind of procrastination that I think matters more than all the rest, and the Bible has a lot to say about it.

We put off many things we know we should do, but some of us put off the biggest one of all: dealing with God. We keep meaning to pray more, to take faith seriously, to actually think about who Jesus is and what He's asking of us. We tell ourselves we'll sort it out when life calms down. After the busy season. After this next thing. We're not saying no. We're just saying *not yet.*

Proverbs warns, "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring" (27:1). And the New Testament carries the same urgency into matters of the soul. "Encourage one another daily, as long as it is called 'Today,' so that none of you may be hardened by sin's deceitfulness" (Hebrews 3:13). Notice that word, *hardened.* Delay doesn't leave us where we started. Each "later" makes the next "later" easier, until a heart that once felt tender has quietly gone quiet. Paul puts it plainly: "now is the time of God's favor, now is the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2).
Rest That Isn't Earned

Here's the good news that makes all this bearable. Jesus doesn't call procrastinators to try harder to be good enough. He says, "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28).

On the cross, He said, "It is finished" (John 19:30). The work that mattered most, the work of making you right with God, is done. You don't have to earn your way to the table. You don't have to clean up the overgrown field before He'll step into it. You can come as you are, weeds and all, and let Him do what you've been unable to do yourself.

And once you're resting in that, you find something strange begins to happen. The things you've been avoiding stop feeling like giants. You're no longer working to prove yourself, so you can simply work, one small step at a time, from a place of peace instead of dread.
So whatever's been sitting on your list the longest, start there. Not because you have to, and not to earn anything, but because you're loved, and because today is the day you actually have.
The thief only wins when we keep saying "later." You don't have to.

items: What has been sitting on your list the longest, and what is it really about? Is it laziness, fear of failing, or simply feeling overwhelmed? What is one small step you could take on it today?

Where do you see the "little sleep, little slumber" pattern in your own life? Think of an area (a relationship, a habit, your health, your work) where small delays have quietly added up. What would one small start look like there this week?
Is there a "not yet" you've been giving God? What would it look like to answer Him today instead of waiting for life to calm down?

blocks.text: Lord, You know the things I've been putting off, the big ones and the small ones. Forgive me for the delay, and forgive me for the times I've put You off too. Give me the courage to take one small step today, and the peace to know I'm doing it from Your love and not out of fear. Thank You that the work that matters most is already finished. Amen.
